usage_en:
Used to ask what someone does for fun. It's one of the standard questions when you're getting to know a Korean person.

Rule: 취미 (hobby) takes 가 here, so it's 취미가 뭐예요? Among close friends the casual form is 취미가 뭐야?

examples.en: What are your hobbies these days?
What are your hobbies? Mine is photography!

usage_en:
A quick way to say you feel the same. It works after almost any statement, positive or negative.

Rule: 저도요 is the polite form; among friends say 나도. If you're agreeing with something the other person doesn't like, 저도요 still works — 저도요, 저도 안 좋아해요.

Used to say something didn't meet your expectations, without being blunt about it.

Rule: 별로예요 is much softer than 싫어요 (I hate it), so Koreans use it to turn things down politely. The topic goes straight in front with no particle — 이 드라마 별로예요.

Used to suggest taking a picture with someone.

Rule: Korean uses 찍다 (to shoot) for taking photos, never 만들다 or 가지다. Put the place in front with 에서 — 여기서 같이 사진 찍어요.

literal_en: Did the photo turn out well?
usage_en:
Used to ask whether a picture came out nicely — a natural follow-up after taking one.

Rule: Korean says a photo 나오다 (comes out) rather than 되다. 잘 나왔어요 means it turned out well, and 잘 안 나왔어요 means it didn't.

Used when you meet someone again after a while.

Rule: This is past tense (지냈어요), asking about the time since you last met. To ask how someone is right now, use 잘 지내요?

Used to ask a friend how something went — a trip, an exam, a first day.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is 어땠어요? Put the topic straight in front with no particle — 시험 어땠어?

literal_en: It was my first time, but ~
usage_en:
Used to set up a contrast between a first experience and how it actually went.

Rule: -인데 attaches background information that the next clause turns around. The polite form is 처음이었는데요, and for something that is your first time right now, use 처음인데.

Used to soften a guess or an opinion so it doesn't sound like a flat assertion. Koreans use it constantly to stay polite.

Rule: The ending changes with the word type. Verbs take -을 것 같아요 for a guess about the future (갈 것 같아요), adjectives take -은/-ㄴ 것 같아요 (좋은 것 같아요), and for the past use -은 것 같아요 (간 것 같아요).

Used to guess about someone else's situation from what you can see or hear.

Rule: Verbs take -나 봐요 (오나 봐요). Adjectives take -은가/-ㄴ가 봐요 — 좋은가 봐요 after a consonant, 바쁜가 봐요 after a vowel. Use it about others, not about your own feelings.

literal_en: I have to ~ / You have to ~
usage_en:
Used to say something is necessary or unavoidable.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is 해야 해요. Attach -아/어야 하다 to a verb stem — 먹어야 해, 가야 해. Adding 꼭 (definitely) in front makes it stronger.

Used to tell a friend not to do something. It sounds caring rather than harsh, depending on tone.

Rule: This is casual speech; the polite form is -지 마세요. Attach -지 말다 to a verb stem — 걱정하지 마, 늦지 마.

Used to ask someone's opinion on a specific topic.

Rule: Put the topic straight in front with no particle. Korean asks 어떻게 생각해요? (how do you think), never 무엇을 생각해요? — the 어떻게 is fixed.

examples.en: What do you think about Korean food?
What do you think about this drama?
What do you think about my plan?

usage_en:
Used to acknowledge that what the other person said makes sense, even if you go on to disagree.

Rule: 맞는 말이에요 agrees with the statement rather than the person. To agree with the person themselves, say 맞아요 or 저도 그렇게 생각해요.

Used to state your own preference without contradicting anyone directly — a gentle way to disagree.

Rule: 좀 (a bit) is what softens it. Dropping it — 저는 달라요 — sounds much more blunt.

Used to ask whether someone has ever visited a place.

Rule: 에 marks the destination, and -아/어 봤어요 adds the sense of having tried it. The answer is 가 봤어요 (I have) or 안 가 봤어요 (I haven't).

Used to recommend a place strongly.

Rule: 꼭 means 'without fail' and carries the emphasis. -아/어 보세요 means 'give it a try', so 가 보세요 is warmer than the plain 가세요.

literal_en: What are you watching these days?
usage_en:
Used to ask what shows someone is into lately — one of the easiest ways to start a conversation.

Rule: 보다 covers watching and reading alike, so it works for dramas, films, and webtoons. 요즘 means 'these days' and goes at the front.

Used when something has completely pulled you in — a drama, a hobby, a genre of music.

Rule: The thing you're hooked on takes 에 — 케이팝에 완전 빠져들었어요. 완전 (totally) is casual emphasis and can be dropped in formal speech.

literal_en: I can't wait for the next episode.
usage_en:
Used to say you're looking forward to what comes next.

Rule: 화 is the counter for episodes, so 다음 화 means 'the next episode'. 기대되다 describes the feeling arising in you, so it takes 가 rather than 를 — 다음 화가 기대돼요.

Used to ask whether someone recognizes a song.

Rule: The negative of 알아요 is 몰라요, not 안 알아요 — Korean uses a separate word. So the answer is 알아요 or 몰라요.

examples.en: Do you know this song? I love it so much!
Do you know this singer's songs?

usage_en:
Used to ask what a line of a song means — a natural question when you're learning through music.

Rule: 무슨 뜻이에요? asks for the meaning of a word or phrase. Put the part you're asking about in front with 가/이 — '그리워'가 무슨 뜻이에요?

Used to ask whether a product or method really makes a difference.

Rule: 효과 (effect) pairs with 있다 and 없다, not with 하다 — say 효과 있어요? and 효과 없어요, never 효과 해요.

Used to say something is well reviewed. Koreans check 후기 before buying almost anything.

Rule: 후기 (review) takes 가 with 좋아요 — 후기가 좋아요. To give the reason for buying, use 후기가 좋아서.

Used to ask about the frequency of a habit or activity.

Rule: 얼마나 (how much) combines with 자주 (often) to ask frequency. Put the verb at the end — 얼마나 자주 운동해요?

Used to say something benefits your health — a very common remark about food in Korea.

Rule: 에 marks what the thing is good for, so the pattern is ~에 좋아요. The same shape works elsewhere — 피부에 좋아요 means 'it's good for your skin'.

Used to ask where someone lives. Koreans often narrow it down by area — 서울 어디 살아요?

Rule: 살다 normally takes 에서 for the place, but with 어디 the particle is dropped in speech. Use the present tense 살아요, not the past.
